Dereserved forest areas 
*266. SHRI DRUPAD BORGOHAIN: Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) the policy of Government to allot Periodic Deeds to the occupants 
in the dereserved forest areas of Assam; 
(b) whether Government have decided to issue periodical pattas to 
the occupants in dereserved land of a thousand bighas in Rangali Forest 
Reserve and sixteen thousand bighas in Panidihing Forest Reserve of 
Sivasagar district of Assam; 
(c) if so, what is the time-frame; and 
(d) whether Government have any policy to convert forest villages 
into revenue villages in near future? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
(a) to (c) There is no scope for allotment of Periodic Deeds by the 
Government in the dereserved forest areas as the subject matter pertains 
to the jurisdiction of the State Government. Government consider the 
diversion of forest areas for non-forestry purposes on merit on getting 
proposals recommended by the State Governments and after examining 
the same as per the rules and guidelines under Forest (Conservation) 
Act, 1980. The Government of Assam has informed that there is no such 
policy for allotment of Periodic Deeds in the dereserved areas. As informed 
by the State Government, there is no reserved forest called Rangali. As 
regard Panidihing Reserved Forest, the State Government has informed 
that the 5632.34 acres have been dereserved and handed over to the 
Revenue Department. 
(d) Government issued detailed guidelines for conversion of all forest 
villages in the country into revenue villages on 18th September, 1990.

Ecological parks in Gujarat 
*262. SHRI BACHANI LEKHRAJ: Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have set up any ecological parks in the 
country particularly in Gujarat; 
(b) if so, the details and main features thereof; 
(c) whether there is any proposal to set up more ecological parks in 
the country; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof, State-wise? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) to (d) There is no provision under the Wild Life (Protection) 
Act, 1972, the Indian Forests Act, 1927 and the Environment (Protection)

including in the State of Gujarat. There is no proposal under consideration 
of Government to set up "ecological parks" in India.

[19 December, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
Wildlife trade 
*265. SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a Delhi-based NGO, Wildlife Trust of India, 
conducted a study into wildlife trade in 2002 in Uttaranchal and U.P.; if 
so, what were its findings; and 
(b) whether Government are thinking of having dialogue with Chinese 
and Nepalese Governments in this regard so that wildlife conservation is 
effectively taken care of? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) Yes, Sir. The Wild Life Trust of India, with the assistance of 
the forest and police officials of the States of Uttar Pradesh and 
Uttaranchal, conducted a study on wildlife trade during the year 2001 -
2002. The important findings of the study are given in the enclosed 
Statement {See below). 
(b) Government have bilateral arrangements with the Chinese and 
Nepalese Governments for effective conservation of "wildlife. A protocol 
on the conservation of the tiger has been signed between Government 
and the Governmet of People's Republic of China. Regular trans boundary 
consultative meetings are held with the Government of Nepal on 
biodiversity conservation. 
Statement 
Important findings of the studies on wildlife trade conducted by Wildlife 
Trust of India 
(i) The trade in wildlife, its products and derivatives, is driven by 
demand from across the borders. 
(ii) Criminals engaged in wildlife crimes are highly organized having 
strong international nexus. Wildlife goods are being exchanged 
for arms and narcotics. 
(iii) India's international border with Nepal and China is highly porous 
thereby providing safe passage to the smugglers. 
(iv) The traders use waterways for illegal shipment of wildlife from 
Uttar Pradesh via West Bengal to Bangladesh. 
41 

RAJYA SABHA [19 December, 2003] 
(v) Seizures during the last few y ears reveal that the enforcement 
agenpies are much more pro-active. 
(vi) Chinese Government, at the request of the Indian Government, 
has officially banned the use of tiger bones. 
(vii) Tibetan refugees settled all over India exploi t the mysticism 
regarding Tibetan medicines especially amongst the poor un-
educated people for using such medicines derived from wild animal 
parts and products. 
(viii) The State of Uttaranchal is a critical area for wildlife trade because 
of its border with Nepal and Tibet. 
(ix) Leopard bones are being sold in the illegal market as a substitute 
for tiger bones 
(x) Alternative livelihood to the hunting and gathering tribes like 
kanjars, bahellias, ma daris, chirimars etc.  can help in curbing 
poaching in illegal trade. 
(xi) Recycling of revenue raised from tourism and other activities can 
be directed towards anti-poaching and anti-trade activities. 
(xii) Immunity may be given to the field staff for use of fire arms under 
Criminal Procedure Code. 
(xiii) Enhancing anti-trade reward scheme through use of secret service 
fund will help in curbing the illegal trade. 
(xiv) There is a need to maintain a Central Data Bank for Wildlife Crimes. 
(xv) Sensitization of judiciary will be highly useful in disposal of wildlife 
offence cases.

Similipal Tiger Reserve 
*272. SHRI RAMACHANDRA KHUNTIA: Will the Minister of 
ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS be pleased to state: 
(a) how many families are yet to be shifted out from inside the 
designated core area of the Similipal Tiger Reserve and how many families 
have already been shifted out; 
(b) whether it is a fact that the wild dogs, cuon alpinus, are slowly 
becoming extinct in the Similipal forests; and 
(c) if so, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) As reported by the State Government, out of 157 families 
from 4 villages within the Similipal Tiger Reserve, 72 families have been 
rehabilitated and 85 families are yet to be relocated. 
(b) and (c) No scientific evidence has come to light indicating that 
the wild dogs in Similipal Tiger Reserve are threatened with extinction.

SUKHDEV SINGH DHINDSA): (a) and (b) Statement is laid on the Table

Statement 
(c) and (d) No case has come to the notice of the National 
Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) where the patients have to pay 
several hundred times more than the actual cost of the common drugs. 
The 74 bulk drugs specified in the First Schedule of the Drugs (Prices 
Control) Order, 1995 (DPCO,95) and the formulations based thereon are 
under price control and their prices  are fixed/revised by NPPA in 
accordance with the provisions of  the DPCO,95. Para 7 of DPCO,95 
gives formula for the calculation of the retail price of a formulation by 
NPPA and it provides for inclusion in the retail price of Maximum Allowable 
Post-manufacturing Expenses (MAPE) not exceeding 100% for 
indigenously manufactured formulations. MAPE means all costs incurred 
by a manufacturer from the stage of ex-factory  cost to retailing and 
includes trade margin and margin for the manufacturer. Similarly, in case 
of an imported formulation, the landed cost forms the basis for fixing its 
price by NPPA alongwith such margin  to cover selling and distribution 
expenses including interest and importer's profit which should not exceed 
fifty percent of the landed cost. Pr ices of non-scheduled formulations 
are fixed by the manufacturers themselves keeping in view the various 
factors like cost of production, marketing/selling expenses, R&D

Crop estimates 
*275. SHRI ABU ASIM AZMI: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) latest estimate of production of major agricultural commodities 
during the current year 2003-04; 
(b) actual production during the preceding year; 
(c) what are the reasons for the rise/fall; and 
(d) whether there is a rise in per capita availability of foodgrains, 
considering the mid-year estimate of population, as compared to last 
year? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI RAJNATH SINGH): 
(a) and (b) The estimated production of foodgrains; oilseeds, cotton, 
jute and sugarcane during 2003-04 vis-a-vis 2002-03 may be seen 
from the enclosed Statement (See below). As per the First Advance 
Estimates for Kharif crops of 2003-04, the production of Kharif rice is 
75.05 million tonnes, which is 12.8% more than the estimated Kharif 
rice production of 2002-03. The prod uction of Kharif coarse cereals is 
estimated at 27.96 million tonnes, which is 38.9% more than the 
corresponding production level of la st year. The production of Kharif 
pulses during 2003-04 is estimated at 5.44 million tonnes, which is 
41.7% more than the corresponding figure last year while the production 
of Kharif oilseeds is estimated at 15.08 million tonnes, which is 63.6% 
more than the corresponding figure last year. In the case of cotton and 
jute also, the estimated production in 2003-04 is higher than that in 
2002-03. However, the estimated pr oduction of sugarcane at 261.37 
million tonnes during 2003-04 is 6. 2% less than the last year's 
production, which reflects the fall in production of sugarcane in 
Maharashtra due to incidence of pests. 
(c) The favourable rainfall received from the South-West monsoon 
contributed significantly to higher production of agricultural commodities

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE

by Dr. M.S. Swaminathan advocates the approach of "Food with Human 
Dignity", in which the poor should be treated as partners in achieving the 
aim of ensuring that each one receives an opportunity for a productive 
and healthy life. The main elements of the plan may be summarized as 
under:— 
(i)      Decentralized implementation. 
(ii)     Intensification of Food for Work approach by inclusion 
of non-manual work also and stepping up the out-lays. 
(iii) Spr ead of awareness about nutrition. 
(iv) House-hold Entitlement Cards. 
(v) Skill upgradations through Training. 
(vi) Setting up of Mal-nutrition Trust of India. 
(vii) Transparent Monitoring. 
(viii) Setting up of Fodder and Feed Banks. 
(ix) Immediate attention to "hunger not-spots". 
(x)    Increase in investment for Agriculture and Rural 
Development. 
(xi)   Shift of strategy to job-led growth.

of programmes and scheme for eradication of poverty, generation of 
employment, improvement in food security and enhancement of nutritional 
status of vulnerable groups etc. being implemented by various Ministries 
of the Central Government and the State Governments etc. The Planning 
Commission is also endeavouring to accommodate the suggestions in 
the above plan as also recommendatio ns made by other scholars in

1895. SHRI SWARAJ KAUSHAL: Will the Minister of ENVIRONMENT 
AND FORESTS be pleased to refer to answer to Unstarred Question 
3760 given in the Rajya Sabha on the 25th April, 2003 and state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that plastic/polythene is harmful to ecology, 
human beings and animals; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that the production/import of plastic and 
polythene has gone up each year during last 3 years; 
107 

RAJYA SABHA [19 December, 2003] 
(c) if so, whether Government will assure that the production/import 
is reduced in the current and next year; and 
(d) if so, how and to what extent, if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) Plastics in general and Polyethylene in particular are 
chemically inert materials, used for the manufacture of a large number of 
consumer items. However, indiscriminate littering of plastics is known to 
cause adverse impacts on ecology, human beings and animals. 
(b) Yes, Sir. As per the information provided by the Indian Center for 
the Plastics in the Environment, the production/imports of plastics have 
gone up during last three years. 
(c) and (d) There is no such proposal with Government. However, to 
discourage indiscriminate littering and to promote proper collection, 
segregation, re-use and recycling of plastics, Government have taken 
several initiatives including the following: 
(i) Recycled Plastics Manufacture and Usage (Amendment) Rules, 
2003, have been notified (vide S.O. 689 (E) dated 17th June, 2003) to 
prohibit the manufacturing, stocking, di stribution or selling of virgin or 
recycled plastic carry bags which are less than 8" x 12" in size and 
thickness less than 20 microns. 
(ii) Import of Scrap plastic of non halogenated polymers and 
copolymers has been restricted under the Hazardous Wastes

Kyoto Protocol 
1900. SHRI PREM CHAND GUPT A: Will the Minister of

(a) whether it is a fact that th e Kyoto Protocol commits developed 
countries to reduce their Green House Gas (GHG) emission to 5 per cent 
below the 1990 level by 2012; 
(b) whether part of these cuts  will be achieved through Clean 
Development Mechanism (CDM), an agreement which allows industrialized 
countries to invest in green projects in developing countries to earn credit 
for their gas emission; and

THE MINISTER OF ENVIRONMENT AND FORESTS (SHRI T.R. 
BAALU): (a) The Kyoto Protocol commits the developed country parties

approximately 5.2% below 1990 levels over the period 2008-2012.

parties would take up Green House Gas reduction project activities in a 
developing country. To enable partici pation in this process, a country 
should be a party to the Kyoto Protocol. The Clean Development 
Mechanism shall be subject to authority and guidance of the Conference 
of Parties serving as the Meeting of  the Parties to the Kyoto Protocol 
and will be supervised by an Executive Board of the Clean Development 
Mechanism.

Meeting of UNESCO 
1940. SHRI B.J. PANDA: Will the Minister of HUMAN RESOURCE 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether UNESCO has held their meet in Delhi recently; and 
(b) if so, the agenda of the meet and salient observations made by 
the participant countries in the field of education? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HUMAN 
RESOURCE DEVELOPMENT (DR. VALLABHBHAI RAMJIBHAI 
KATHIRIA): (a) Yes, sir. The third meeting of the High Level Group on 
Education For All (EFA) was co-hosted by India and UNESCO from 10th 
to 12th November, 2003. Sixteen countries participated in this meet. 
(b) The main agenda of this meet was to discuss: 
(i) Review of progress on EFA goals set in Dakar; 
(ii) Action agenda for achieving gender goals; 
(iii) National planning and policy reform; 
(iv) International action for support and financing of EFA; and 
(v) Challenges and opportunities:The path ahead. 
151 

RAJYA SABHA [19 December, 2003] 
The salient observations made by the participating countries in the 
field of education, inter-alia, included: 
(i) All participating countries agreed that there was a need to set up 
efforts for girls' education to achieve the gender equality at primary 
stage by 2005 and the gender parity goal by 2015; 
(ii) Many of the participating countries agreed that the projections 
made and inferences drawn in the Global Monitoring Report on 
Education For AII-2003 were based on old data. There was call for 
the UNESCO Institute of Statistics (UIS) to fine tune their estimation 
methods to include updated survey data and not wait for 
disaggregated census data. It was felt that UIS also needs to 
enhance its capacity for analysis and forecasting so that the 
conclusions drawn by it can be more realistic. 
(iii) Donor countries and international agencies should fulfil their 
commitments made at Dakar and Monterrey. This referred to the 
need to substantially step up their Official Development Assistance 
(to reach 0.7% of their GNP) and increase the allocation therefrom 
to Elementary Education.

Statement 
Details of steps taken by Government for the protection of Child Rights 
and to award punishments in cases of torture and sexual abuse of 
children 
(c) Action to protect child rights is undertaken by several Ministries/ 
Departments in the Government of India such as: 
(i)  Department of Women and Child Development 
157 

RAJYA SABHA [19 December, 2003] 
(ii)  Ministry of Health and Family Welfare 
(iii)  Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment 
(iv)  Ministry of Labour. 
The Government has enacted various legislations from time to time 
to safeguard the rights of children against sexual abuse, violence and 
inhuman treatment. These laws can be categorized under three broad 
sections: 
(1) Crimes committed against children which are punishable under 
Indian Penal Code (IPC), which include (i) kidnapping for exporting (section 
360 IPC), (ii) kidnapping from lawful guardianship (section 361 IPC), (iii) 
kidnapping for compel for marriage (section 366 IPC), (iv) procuration of 
minor girls (induced or seduced or forc ed to illicit intercourse) (section 
366-A of IPC), (v) selling of girls for prostitution (section 372 of IPC), (vi) 
buying of girls for prostitution (sec tion 373 of IPC), (vii) Rape (section 
375 of IPC) and (viii) unnatural offences (section 377 of IPC). 
(2) Crimes against children which are punishable under Special Laws, 
which include: (i) Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act (where minors are abused 
in prostitution), (ii) Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986; 
and (iii) Child Marriage Restraint Act, 1929. 
(3) Protective legislations to protect the children from exploitation 
and vulnerabilities, which include, (i) Factories Act, 1948, (ii) Hindu 
Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956, (iii) Hindu Adoption and Maintenance 
Act, 1956, (iv) The Infant Milk Substitutes Feeding Bottles and Infant 
Foods (Regulation of Production, Supply and Distribution) Act, 1992, (v) 
Pre-conception and Pre-natal Diagnostic Techniques (Prohibition of Sex 
Selection) Act, 2002, (vi) Persons with Disabilities (Equal Opportunities, 
Protection of Rights and Full Participation) Act, 1996 and (vii) Juvenile 
Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2000.

THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF STEEL (SHRI 
BRAJ KISHORE TRIPATHY): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The proposal for disinvestment in RINL is based on the 
recommendations of Disinvestment Commission contained in its Xllth 
Report which are as follows:- 
(i) the entire accumulated losses  of the Company of Rs. 4065.30 
crores as on 31.03.1999 should be written off by the Government against 
its entire share money pending allotment and preference share capital 
and a part of the equity capital to clean up its balance sheet and keep 
the company from being referred to BIFR; and 
(ii) simultaneously to initiate process of disinvestment of not less 
than 51% of its remaining equity holding  in RINL to a strategic buyer. 
In view of the strengths of the plant, the Commission feels that the 
investor interest in acquiring RINL after the balance sheet is cleaned up. 
The selection of strategic buyer should be done through global competitive 
bidding by pre-qualification of bidders. 
Disinvestment Commission has given the following reasons for their 
above mentioned recommendations:- 
(i) The Disinvestment Commission classified RINL as non-core 
and opined that no public purpose would be served retaining 
RINL under Government ownership. 
(ii) Steel Industry in India is completely decontrolled with the 
presence of large number of private producers. Imports are 
freely permitted with declining import duties. Hence, the 
Steel market is fully contestable not only vis-a-vis Indian 
producers but also other steel majors in the world. The public 
sector steel industry in Indi a would, therefore, have to 
compete in the highly compet itive and technology/market 
driven international steel sector. Since public sector form of 
management does not allow such flexibility/investments it 
would be advisable to disinvest majority Government equity 
in RINL. 
(iii) RINL has distinct advantages of its location, layout, technology 
and should be an ideal steel plant in India for 
198 

[19 December, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
steel majors in the world to invest in. With proper restructuring      
the plant can be converted into a 10 million tonne export oriented 
plant by one of the international steel majors. 
(iv) The next steel upturn is expected in 2002 and plant should be 
disinvested looking at the time of the next steel upturn. 
(v) The Disinvestment Commissi on felt that the company needed 
substantial financial support from Government of India for 
financial restructuring and expansion and that as this would 
involve huge cash, outflow from Government, this would not 
be justified and is avoidable. It was further of the view that 
capital expansion in the steel plant would be more expensive 
in terms of time and money if undertaken while remaining 
under Government of India control.

AND SPORTS (SHRI VIJAY GOEL): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. The Anti-doping

centrally sponsored scheme of Government of India called "Scheme for 
Dope Test". The Government has launched the scheme for dope test in 
the Tenth Five Year Plan with the objectives: (i) to have an International 
Olympic Committee-accredited Dope Control Centre in India (ii) to maintain 
quality control system as requi red by International standard, i.e., ISO 
17025 (iii) to educate athletes, coaches and other supporting personnel

certification which are mandatory re quirements as per International

suspend Sh. Abhijit Kale from parti cipating in any tournament. On the 
issue of suspension of Sh. Kale, the matter is also pending before the 
Bombay High Court.

Promotion of sports among women 
2005. SHRI DARA SINGH: Will the Mi nister of YOUTH AFFAIRS AND SPORTS 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that out of 18 spor ts hostels of the Sports Authority of India 
there is only one sports hostel for women and no exclusive SPDA hostel for girls; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that not mu ch has been done by sports federations for 
development of sports among Indian women as compared to China and other European 
countries; and 
216 

[19 December, 2003]       RAJYA   SABHA 
(c) if so, what incentives, sports facilities by openi ng more sports 
hostel and cash awards/medals are proposed to be given by Government, 
so as to attract mass participation by women? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF YOUTH AFFAIRS 
AND SPORTS (SHRI VIJAY GOEL): (a) No, Sir. The erstwhile of Sports 
Project Development Area (SPDA) and the Sports Hostel Scheme of 
Sports Authority of India (SAI) were merged by SAI in 1955 and a new 
scheme viz., SAI Training Centre was launched. Under the Scheme, 
presently, there are 58 SAI Training Centres all over the country, out of 
which four are exclusively for girls and in rest of the Centres, training is 
being imparted to both boys and girls trainees. 
(b) No, Sir. National Sports Federations and the Government are 
giving equal importance to the prom otion of sports among women as 
among men. The efforts include regular conduct of National level 
championships in both senior and junior categories, training and foreign 
exposure. 
(c) Cash awards/incentives are being provided to women sports 
persons for their performance in international sports events at par with 
men. A Sports Festival for women is organised annually by the Sports 
Authority of India (SAI) to encourage mass participation of women in 
sports. The Sports Scholarship Scheme being implemented by SAI 
also envisages special scholarships for women.

CALLING ATTENTION TO MATTER OF URGENT PUBLIC 
IMPORTANCE 
The plight of tea garden workers due to sickness and closure of a 
large number of tea gardens leading to starvation deaths 
SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE (West Bengal): Madam, with your 
permission, I call the attention of the Minister of Commerce and Industry 
to the plight of tea garden workers due to sickness and closure of a large 
number of tea gardens leading to starvation deaths. 
244 

[19 December, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE AND THE MINISTER OF 
COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI ARUN JAITLEY): Madam Deputy 
Chairperson, the domestic tea indust ry is faced with a situation of 
continuously falling tea prices at auctions for the last four years. The 
average auction prices of tea were about Rs. 76 per kilogram in 1998. 
They started declining from mid- 1999 onwards. Presently, they have 
reached about Rs. 55 per kilogram. Domestic prices of tea move more or 
less in tandem with the international prices. These prices have remained 
depressed over the last few years due to the over supply of tea in the 
global market. They declined from about US$ 1.88 per kilogram in 1998 
to US$ 1.32 per kilogram in 2002. This decline in international prices 
coupled with problems like decreasing exports, sluggish rate of growth 
of domestic demand, and higher cost of production has adversely affected 
the domestic tea industry. 
Individual tea gardens, particularly the medium sized ones and those 
financially weak, have been severely affected by the decline in prices, 
especially because the cost of production continues to be high. Some 
tea gardens are sick and some have closed down in the States of West 
Bengal, Kerala, Assam and Tripura. As per information available, 43 tea 
gardens are presently closed. Of these, 25 are in West Bengal, 12 in 
Kerala and 3 each in Assam and Tripura. More than, 35,000 workers are 
affected by the closure. Recently, 36 closed gardens were got studied by 
Expert Committees appointed by the Government of India. The reports 
of these Committees indicate that these gardens have been inherently 
weak, which have suffered from chronic low yields and poor garden 
management and, in many cases, strained industrial relations. The fall in 
the prices of tea hastened their cl osure. From the information made 
available by the State Governments of West Bengal and Kerala, where 
most of these closed gardens are located, there has been no starvation 
death due to their closure. 
The Plantation Labour Act, 1951 provides for the welfare of plantation 
labour and regulates the conditions of work in plantations. This Act specifies 
the facilities to be provided to the workers, including drinking water, 
housing, educational and medical facilities. The State Governments are 
responsible for the administration and implementation of the Plantation 
Labour Act. The Government of India have already taken up this matter 
with the concerned State Governments for intervention and providing 
245 

RAJYA SABHA [19 December, 2003] 
necessary relief. Some State Governments like West Bengal and Kerala 
have taken steps to provide relief to  the affected plantation workers. 
Steps taken include creation of employment opportunities from various 
schemes such as the Sampoorna Grameena Rozgar Yojana, extended 
health care, implementing nutritional programmes for the children, 
distribution of foodgrains, augmenting drinking water facilities and 
distribution of cash to the most needy. The Government of India is fully 
alive to the problems confronting t he tea industry. Several steps have 
been taken to support the tea industry. As already mentioned, Expert 
Committees were constituted to study in depth 36 closed gardens. 
According to the Reports of thes e Committees, all these estates are 
required to invest both in the plantations as well as in the factory and 
other infrastructure to achieve better results in terms of quantity, quality 
and price realisation of their teas. However, bulk of the investment is 
required in the plantation itself. The Government has facilitated discussions 
by the managements of these gardens with their bankers to work out a 
revival package. This package would include promoters' contribution, 
further loans from concerned banks with restructuring of the accounts 
and also assistance from the Central Government. The assistance would 
be in the form of an interest subsidy up to a maximum of 5 per cent for 
those gardens which are considered financially viable by the concerned 
banks. 
Other measures taken by the Go vernment to provide necessary 
support to the tea industry, include the following: 
(a) The excise duty of Re. 1/- per kilogram on tea has been replaced 
by an additional duty of excise of Re. 1/- per kilogram as a surcharge, 
which would form a fund for the development, modernisation and 
rehabilitation of the tea plantation sector. Assistance, through this fund, 
would be extended for providing interest subsidy to closed gardens which 
are potentially viable, increasing pr oduction of orthodox tea, generic 
promotion of tea and research and development. The schemes are being 
finalised for implementation. 
(b) Implementation of a number of developmental schemes during 
the Tenth Five Year Plan by the T ea Board for enhancing productivity, 
quality and marketability of tea produc ed in the country. Financial and 
technical assistance is being provided for various plantation development 
246 

[19 December, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
activities like replanting, rejuvenation, creation of irrigation facilities, etc. 
An outlay of Rs. 350 crores has been provided in the Tenth Plan for Tea 
Board for this purpose. 
(c) A Price Stabilisation Fund with an initial corpus of Rs. 500 crores 
has been established for providing relief to the small growers of plantation 
commodities such as tea, coffee, rubber and tobacco. 
(d) Government has moved the RBI and the Indian Banks Association 
for providing an effective credit relief package for the tea industry from 
the banking sector. 
(e)Tea Board is in the process of implementing an IT based Information 
Dissemination Plan for the tea industry, including electronisation of auction 
centres. This would improve the efficiency of the tea purchase systems 
and reduce transaction time and costs. 
(f) In order to promote exports of tea, financial assistance is provided 
to tea exporters to meet part of the cost of handling, packaging, transport/ 
freight and value addition, even as efforts are being made to improve the 
quality of teas produced in the country through a quality upgradation 
programme being implemented by the Tea Board. 
(g) Promotional support is being lent to Indian exporters in their 
promotion and marketing of tea brands. 
(h) The import duty on items of machinery used to improve productivity 
and quality of tea, including value addition, has been reduced to an all 
inclusive rate of 5 per cent. 
(i) An Inter-Ministerial Committee, set up by the Ministry of Labour, 
has also studied the issues relating to the plantation sector, particularly 
the social costs, provident fund dues of the plantation workers and 
taxation structures. The recommendations of this Committee are under 
consideration. 
Besides these measures, the Government has also got a study 
conducted on the primary marketing system for tea, including the auction 
system. Based on the study, Government has notified the Tea Marketing 
Control Order, 2003 and modified the auction rules in order to bring about 
greater transparency in the price discovery mechanism for tea. Due to 
these changes, there has been a saving in transaction time and cost in 
247 

RAJYA SABHA [19 December, 2003] 
selling teas through the auctions resulting in larger volumes of tea being 
sold in a shorter periods of time. 
I am happy to inform the House that there has been greater absorption 
of tea in the domestic market and the overall supply and demands 
imbalance has been greatly reduced. In fact, sales in the North Indian 
auctions, since November, 2003, have started showing better price trends 
particularly for the good quality teas. Overall improvement in productivity, 
cost reduction, a conscious effort towards the production of quality teas 
and better management practices would go a long way in reviving the 
tea industry and ensuring welfare of the workers.

DR. M.N. DAS (Orissa): Thank you, Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir. I shall 
be very brief. If I recollect correctl y, I was, perhaps, referring to the 
contradiction in our soci al culture. On the one hand, we sholwed our 
reverance and regard to womanhood by addressing them as devis or 
Goddnesses; but, on the other hand, we prepetuated inhuman atrocities 
on them, beginning from female infanticide to widow buring-widow may 
be of any age and the husband may be  of any age. But that is an old 
story. Let us come to today. Today, what is happening to our sisters any 
daughters? We are worried about the present time. We are talking of 
water pollution, air pollution, etc. But, today, the greatest threat to India 
is that of pollution of social environment. Our society is heading to some 
kind of perversion. Before we think of preventive and curative measures, 
we will have to go into the causes in these types of social maladies. In 
my opinion, if we trace the causes of the pervading social lack of moral 
values, we find there is some kind of Western invasion on Indian culture. 
At one time, there was a phrase The West is West and the East is East, 
and the twain shall never meet". But that phrase has become outmoded 
and it does not hold any ground today. Because the whole earth is 
described today as 'global village' as cultures know no frontiers. So, the 
East is influenced by the Western culture, and the West is also influenced 
by the Eastern culture. But there is a wide difference between the two 
invasions. Suppose, Indian culture invades the West, but it is only in a 
subtle and indirect manner, touching the fringe of Western society, whether 
it is Swami Vivekanand's Vedantic Mission, or, Mahesh Yogi's meditation 
course, or, ISKON's devotional themes. Such Eastern influences touch 
only the fringe of the Western soci ety. On the other hand, the Western 
culture invades us on a large scale; on a wider scale through the electronic 
media, television channels, Foreign Direct Investment in our Press; print 
media, advertisement, and the various serials that we see every evening 
or everyday on the electronic media. Indirectly, we are coming under the 
impact and influence of Western culture, leading to some kind of vulgarity, 
violence, disco dance, etc. And our adolescents or youth are susceptible 
to such kind of impact on their minds. And that leads to even murders in 
nightclubs, or rapes,-as it happened with a foreign diplomat-and various 
other types of crimes. But, greater than this is our own social apathy 
towards what happens in the society. 
Sir, Police cannot be deployed everywhere to protect every individual. 
270 

[19 December, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA  
We cannot depend on the State Force to detect the places or incidents of 
crime. But social apathy creates a greater problem. 
Some two years back, one incident took place on the streets of Delhi at a 
crowded place. A lady was walking towards the market with a gold chain on 
her neck. Two ruffians pounced upon her to  snatch the chain. She resisted, 
cried, screamed and shouted for help. Passers-by were walking on both sides 
of the street. They stopped and just observed the drama of the attack. She 
was stabbed by the ruffian and was rushed to the hospital. The next day, 
some journalists met her on the sick bed in the hospital. They asked her, "Do 
you feel sad about the stabbing?" Do you know what reply she gave? She 
said, "I don't feel sad for this stabbing or for my wounds or for my health. I feel 
sad that the passers-by stood there silent ly as spectators. I cried hoarse for 
their help. Some of them could have brave enough to rescue me. Some could 
have shouted for the police. Some could have just threathened the hooligans 
to run away, and they might have disappeared at once. But, I feel sad for the 
indifference of the society." So, this new form of social menance has 
developed. We don't come to the rescue of innocent victims suffering from 
injustice or from crime. 
My other point is this. We call ourse lves progressive. Certainly, we are 
progressing. We are spreading education. But, have we been able to replace 
the social vices, social superstitions, blind beliefs, or incidents like innocent 
ladies being stoned to death somewhere in a remote place on suspiction of 
witchcraft? Have we created awareness against these kind of superstitions? 
Have we not replaced Sati Daha system with Badhu Daha, or, widow, buring 
with bride burning? Is the society conscious about such vices? Have we tried 
to creat awareness? So, Sir, I would appeal to the House, or, appeal to the 
society, through the House, that let us create a new awareness against 
prevailing superstitions and crimes, so that our women work feel safe. 
At the same time, I request the Government to take stern action against 
the crimes and abuses that are perpetrated on our women. Both the State and 
the society have to collaborate in eradicating the present permissive social 
system, and the continuing violence against our women. Thank you.

women. I want to draw you kind attention to an incident that occurred in

women are being killed naming them as witch and sometimes also in

In that incident, culprits tied the husband with a tree and before the

of Criminal Statistics, which are Government Reports, in 1997 the total

because they are also physically weak, because they are not earning, they are

their male counterparts. And, because their number is

support the Private Members' Bill of my friend, Smt. Bimba Raikar, namely the 
Women and Girls (Prevention of Stripping,  Teasing, Molestation, branding as

the victims. If we analyse the cases of national capital alone of the 
recent past, we may recall the molestation and rape of a medical student 
of the Maulana Azad Medical College, molestation, rape and blinding of 
a nurse in a nursing home, gang ra pe of a college student by Army 
jawans and molestation and rape of a Swiss diplomat in a moving car. 
Few days back, the media reported that on the election day, two personnel 
of Delhi Police, after completing their duty, were going back. They noticed 
a young girl in her balcony. To become fresh, they simply barged into her 
house, molested and brutally raped her in the presence of her relatives. 
This shocking news that protectors turned culprits has put a question 
mark on the very safety of women. Mo re horrifying aspect of this case 
was the revelation of media that the higher authorities of Delhi Police 
tried their best to hush up the case. Thanks to some women organisation, 
a case has been made out against the policewallas. But apprehensions 
are still there that police will make the case very weak. When Army 
jawans and policemen will be on prowl for the girls and women, what will 
happen to their safety and security? Here, the question arises as to what 
action is taken against the rapist policewallas. Whether hon. Minister 
has any data of policemen involved in rape cases during the last one 
decade, and how many of them have been prosecuted and dismissed? I 
feel, deterrent punishment has to be awarded in such cases and wherever 
the higher-ups try to hush up the cases, they first be summarily dismissed. 
For this, the Government will have to  muster courage and find out the 
black sheep in the uniform. For others or general public, the punishment 
must be stringent and law must be enforced in letter and spirit. But, 
unfortunately, when the question of enforcement of law in cases of women 
comes, the implementation is very, very poor for which the nation and 
our society and law -enforcers have to do introspection for giving justice 
to women. 
Teasing is yet another kind of harassment the girls and women 
have to undergo. The girls and women cannot travel in public transport, 
cannot go to public places because they have to tolerate the obscene 
remarks, body gestures, whist ling and many a time, physical 
annoyance. The teasers are of all kinds-ruffians and even gentlemen, of 
all age groups, be they young or old. They roam around girls' schools, 
women colleges, markets, cinemas, public transport, parks and almost 
everywhere. When the girls and women are teased in public transport 
or place, the general public reacts as mute spectators, which emboldens 
279 

RAJYA  SABHA [19 December, 2003] 
the teasers. Here too, the law an d its enforcement are very weak. I 
understand, a Bill to prevent eve-testing was passed in this very House 
a decade ago which lapsed due to the dissolution of then Lok Sabha,but 
successive Governments did not bother to re-introduce the Bill and get it 
passed. 
Then comes the issue of stripping of women in public places. 
Many a time, news percolates that woman was stripped naked and 
chased in public place. Many a time, this is the result of revenge 
against the women herself or with her family so as to teach a lesson. 
This happens generally in a village where feudalism prevails one way or 
the other who are not afraid of law. But, Sir, it happened even in Karnataka, 
when a dalit woman went to fetch water in a village well, she was stripped 
nude and taken in a procession. Such incidents have to be taken seriously 
by the Government by ensuring that culprits do get exemplary punishment. 
Many a time, news comes that women have been killed after being 
branded as witches. Recently, such incidents were reported from Bihar, 
Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, new, Mr. Khuntia has said, even in Orissa. 
This brutality is a result of superstitions and abetment due to the lust or 
grievance of some influential people in the villages. Such thing should 
also be noted and the Government should take strigent action against 
the people. 
This is very unfortunate that despite the law, the system of Devadasi 
is still prevalent in various parts of the country, including my home-state, 
Karnataka. The Karnataka Legislature had enacted the Devadasi 
(Prohibition of Dedication) Act, 1982, to remove this social evil from the 
State, but stray cases still come to notice. This evil practice destroys 
the lives of innocent girls who ultimately lend into flesh trade. Since the 
root cause of this evil practice is superstition, the Central and the State 
Governments will have to declare a war on this practice. The services of 
NGOs may also be taken in this regard. 
Since the Bill aims to remove various atrocities against girls and 
women, I hope the Government will give a serious thought to the proposals 
of Mrs. Raikar and other speakers on the Bill. I once again support this 
Bill and hope the Government too will support it. 
Thank you, for giving me time to speak on this important Bill.

The next point is teasing. Teasing is a very bad thing. In hostels and 
colleges, where co-education is there, innocent girls are teased by boys 
in a very cruel and rude way. There are incidents where college girls 
committed suicide when they were hurt so badly. How do we prevent it? 
It can't be prevented by giving speeches here by anybody. How should 
the Government do it? Here comes social transformation. College lecturers 
and professors, who are teaching the students, must inculcate in the 
minds of boys and girls that they should not do such things in their life, 
they should not make people to laugh at them, they should never tease 
the girls, make them cry and, sometimes, commit suicide. This kind of 
social transformation should happen in their minds. Therefore, in colleges, 
schools and other places, while giving normal education, this must also 
be inculcated In the minds of the students and the people. Things like 
parading women naked in an innocent, foolish, emotional and fascinating 
way or converting them into Devadasis or beating women, by mistake, 
taking them as witches and killers, are happening. Suddenly, in a village, 
if such things take place, we can't blame the police or the Government 
and ask them why they are not able to prevent them. There is a method 
of prevention, that is, creating awareness in the society. There are some 
NGOs. There are some social orga nisations. There are voluntary 
organisations. There are women voluntary organisations. They must 
preach and inform the villagers and the innocent people that the days 
have changed; don't go in the wrong track; don't be innocent and ignore 
it; it is very unfair and it is totally  a sin to ill-treat women; God will not 
pardon anybody who hurts or ill-treats women foolishly in the name of 
religion, and, therefore, don't do it. This type of a message must go. 
Secondly, the media people, journalists, local tehsildars or 
Government executives must inform the police, if anything takes place 
and action must be taken immediately against the people who are 
responsible for attacking the women, by mistake, taking them as witches 
or converting them into Devadasis or making them walk naked in a foolish 
way. Those who do such things should be punished immediately and 
such things should be prevented by preaching the people. I have got 
some statistics with me. In the month of August, in New Delhi, in 15 
days, I understand, 15 rapes took place. Therefore, at least, in New Delhi 
city the police should be alert How? Of course, it is very difficult to say 
where and when such an incident would happen. Still there is a possibility. 
In such places like the India Gate; bus stands, etc., where much traffic

THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JUSTICE AND THE MINISTER OF 
COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI ARUN JAITELY): Mr. Vice-
Chairman, Sir, the hon. Member has raised a very important issue. And 
even though the issue has been raised in  the context of creation of a 
Bench of the High Court at Surat, the larger ramifications of this issue 
are of extreme importance to the J udicial system. Each State normally 
has one seat, as far as the High Court is concerned. For various reasons, 
in some of the States, particularly the larger States, more than one seat 
has been created. The object of creat ing more than one seat could be 
many. And, one of the obvious criteria is that where distances are very 
large and litigants have to travel a long distance and there are regions 
within a State which are identifiable a little different, then, it would be in 
the interest of Justice, in the interest of cheaper justice, that a Bench of 
the High Court can be created at a point other than where the normal 
seat of the High Court is located, in  fact, there are some States where 
there are more than seat of the High Court, which has been created, 
and this system   itself has functioned well and functioned effectively. 
[THE DEPUTY CHAIRMAN in the Chair] 
The Mumbai High Court, for instance, has a seat at Aurangabad. It 
also has a special Bench in Goa. It has a Bench at Nagpur. In Madhya 
Pradesh, even though the main seat is in Jabalpur, there are special 
Benches created for histroical reasons at Indore and Gwalior. Similarly, 
the principal seat of the High Court of Uttar Pradesh is in Allahabad, but 
it has a special Bench, which has been created in Lucknow. The 
Government, at present, has been functioning with, at least, two State 
Governments with the object of creating special Benches and separate 
Benches in those States. For the High Court, but a Bench is new being 
created and all formalities are complete and we are in the stage where 
infrastructure is being created for a Bench at Madurai. Similarly, in West 
Bengal, in a very harmonious manner, the High Court, the Bar, the State 
Government, the Central Government, have all agreed for the creation 
of the Bench of the West Bengal High Court in addition to the Calcutta 
High Court at Jalpaiguri itself. And, this normally helps the litigants, 
particularly when areas are far-flung and it helps in cutting down the 
cost. However, much that there may be a laudable object of creation of 
304 

[19 December, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
these Benches, there is a particular legal procedure which has to be 
followed in the creation of these Benches and the Government of the 
day is, at present, constrained, as far as that legal procedure is 
concerned. For instance, in the context of Gujarat, the Government 
had appointed a Committee headed by a retired Judge of the Supreme 
Court, Justice Palekar, in 1983 to consider this whole question. Justice 
Palekar went into this whole question and on 23rd August, 1985, he 
submitted a detailed report. Now, I am just giving some of the 
conclusions that Justice Palekar came to in the context of Gujarat. He 
concluded that, "A circuit Bench may be established on the initiative of 
the Chief Justice subject to the Governor's approval under Section 28(3) 
of the Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1960. That is, if a circuit Bench, 
which is not a permanent Bench, is to be established, the Chief Justice 
of the High Court is competent with the permission of the Governor to 
establish that. The Central Government or no other agency comes into 
the picture. The Bombay Re-organisation Act, 1960, does not authorise 
the establishment of a permanent Bench. An amendment of the Act is 
necessary for such an authorisation." But, besides that he further went 
on to opine/There are no historical, geographical or even sentimental 
reasons for establishing a permanent bench anywhere in the State of 
Gujarat. Political considerations for establishment of such a bench are 
irrelevant. If due to local pressures, one yields to such demands from 
one area, pressure will build up from other areas also, and, it will be 
difficult to resist them. In that case, the High Court wilt be crippled and 
loose its integrity and cohesion affecting irretrievably the administration 
of justice in the State." In any event, such an experiment should not be 
attempted in a new High Court, which is too young to build a strong 
tradition of an independent integrity, although, currently it is trying to live 
up to the highest standards. 
Even though this recommendation was given in 1983, and, 20 years 
have passed since then, and, much water has flowed since then, the 
Government of India as such is willing to consider whatever suggestions 
come up before the Government of India, because it is also a fact that 
the population of the State is incr easing, the number of cases is 
increasing, the number of cases pending before the various High Courts 
is piling up, the cost of litigation itself is increasing. Therefore, we have 
always been open as far as suggestion is concerned.

Even though the recommendations of Justice Palekar in July, 1991

creation of a separate Bench in Gujarat, in particular, at places such 
as Rajkot and Surat. There have been also some demands, which 
have come from the city of Baroda for the establishment of a Bench in
